Abstract.

In this article we obtain the classification of the congruences of lines with one-dimensional focal locus. It turns out that one can restrict to study the case of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}.

Key words and phrases:
Algebraic Geometry, Focal loci, Grassmannians, Congruences
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14M15, 14N05, Secondary 51N35

Introduction

A congruence BB of lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} is a family of lines of dimension n−1n-1. The order of BB is the number of lines of BB passing through a general point in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} and its class is the number of lines of the congruence contained in a general hyperplane and meeting a general line contained in it.

The study of congruences of lines in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} was started by E. Kummer in [Kum66], in which he gave a classification of those of order one. More recently, congruences of lines in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} were studied in [Gol85] by N. Goldstein, who tried to classify these from the point of view of their focal locus. The focal locus is, roughly speaking, the set of critical values of the natural map between the total space Λ\Lambda of the family BB and ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. Successively, Z. Ran in [Ran86] studied the surfaces of order one in the general Grassmannian 𝔾⁡(r,n)\mathbb{G}(r,n) i.e. families of rr-planes in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} for which the general (n−r−2)(n-r-2)-plane meets only one element of the family. He gave a classification of such surfaces, in particular, in the case of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}, obtaining a modern and more correct proof of Kummer’s classification of first order congruences of lines. Moreover, he proved that if the class of these congruences in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} is greater than three, these are not smooth, as conjectured by I. Sols. Another proof of Kummer’s classification is given by F. L. Zak and others in [ZILO]. Moreover, E. Arrondo and I. Sols, in [AS92] classified all the smooth congruences with small invariants. Successively, E. Arrondo and M. Gross in [AG93] classified all the smooth congruences in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} with a fundamental curve and this classification was extended to all smooth congruences with a fundamental curve by E. Arrondo, M. Bertolini and C. Turrini in [ABT94].

In this paper the classification of congruences with focal locus of dimension one (i.e. if the focal locus reduces to be only a—possibly reducible or non-reduced—fundamental curve) is obtained. In Section 1 we fix the notation and we recall some known results. In Section 2 we obtain some general results on the possible minimal dimension of the focal locus of a congruence in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}: first of all, we prove in Theorem 2.1 that if the focal locus has codimension at least two, then the congruence has order either zero or one. This result has been suggested to us by F. Catanese. In Theorem 2.2 we prove that the dimension of the focal locus is at least n−12\frac{n-1}{2}—if the congruence is not a star of lines, i.e. the set of lines passing through a point P∈ℙnP\in\mathbb{P}^{n} (in which case the focal locus has support in PP). Moreover, we give also some results concerning the case of dimension n−12\frac{n-1}{2}.

In Section 3 we prove the main result of this paper, namely Theorem 0.1; in order to state it, we need the following notation: first of all, let ℓ\ell be a fixed line in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} and ℙℓ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\ell} the set of the planes containing ℓ\ell. Let ϕ\phi be a general nonconstant morphism from ℙℓ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\ell} to ℓ\ell and let Π\Pi be a general element in ℙℓ1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\ell}. We define ℙϕ⁡(Π),Π1\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\phi(\Pi),\Pi} as the pencil of lines passing through the point ϕ⁡(Π)\phi(\Pi) and contained in Π\Pi.

Theorem 0.1.

If the focal locus FF of a congruence of lines BB in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} has dimension one, then n=2,3n=2,3. If n=2n=2 FF is an irreducible curve of degree greater than one and BB is its dual; if n=3n=3 BB is a first order congruence, and we have the following possibilities:

  1. (1)

    FF is an irreducible curve, which is either:

    1. (a)

      a rational normal curve C3C_{3} in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. In this case BB is the family of secant lines of C3C_{3} and has bidegree (1,3)(1,3) in the Grassmannian;

    2. (b)

      or a non-reduced scheme whose support is a line ℓ\ell, and the congruence is—using the above notation—∪Π∈ℙℓ1ℙ1ϕ⁡(Π),Π\cup_{\Pi\in\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\ell}}\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\phi(\Pi),\Pi}; if we set d:=deg⁡(ϕ)d:=\deg(\phi), the congruence has bidegree (1,d)(1,d); or

  2. (2)

    FF is a reducible curve, union of a line F1F_{1} and a rational curve F2F_{2} such that length⁡(F1∩F2)=deg⁡(F2)−1\length(F_{1}\cap F_{2})=\deg(F_{2})-1; BB is the family of lines meeting F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} and it has bidegree (1,deg⁡(F2))(1,\deg(F_{2})).

1. Notation and Preliminaries

We will work with schemes and varieties over the complex field ℂ\mathbb{C}, with the standard definitions and notation as in [Har77]. For us a variety will always be projective. More information about general results and references about families of lines, focal diagrams and congruences can be found in [De 01b], [De 01a] and [De 00], or [De 99]. Besides, we refer to [GH78] for notation about Schubert cycles and to [Ful84] for the definitions and results of intersection theory. So we denote by σa0,a1\sigma_{a_{0},a_{1}} the Schubert cycle of the lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} contained in a fixed (n−a1)(n-a_{1})-dimensional subspace H⊂ℙnH\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} and which meet a fixed (n−1−a0)(n-1-a_{0})-dimensional subspace Π⊂H\Pi\subset H. Here we recall that a congruence of lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} is a (flat) family (Λ,B,p)(\Lambda,B,p) of lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} obtained as the pull-back of the universal family under the desingularization map of a subvariety B′B^{\prime} of dimension n−1n-1 of the Grassmannian 𝔾⁡(1,n)\mathbb{G}(1,n) of lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. So Λ⊂B×ℙn\Lambda\subset B\times\mathbb{P}^{n} and pp is the restriction of the projection p1:B×ℙn→Bp_{1}:B\times\mathbb{P}^{n}\rightarrow B to Λ\Lambda, while we will denote the restriction of p2:B×ℙn→ℙnp_{2}:B\times\mathbb{P}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n} by ff. Λb:=p−1​(b)\Lambda_{b}:=p^{-1}(b), (b∈B)(b\in B) will be a line of the family and f⁡(Λb)=:Λ⁡(b)f(\Lambda_{b})=:\Lambda(b) is the corresponding line in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. A point y∈ℙny\in\mathbb{P}^{n} is called fundamental if its fibre f−1​(y)f^{-1}(y) has dimension greater than the dimension of the general one. The fundamental locus is the set of the fundamental points. It is denoted by Ψ\Psi. Moreover the locus of the points y∈ℙny\in\mathbb{P}^{n} for which the fibre f−1​(y)f^{-1}(y) has positive dimension will be denoted by Φ\Phi.

Since Λ\Lambda is smooth of dimension nn, we define the focal divisor R⊂ΛR\subset\Lambda as the ramification divisor of ff. The schematic image of the focal divisor RR under ff (see, for example, [Har77]) is the focal locus F⊂ℙnF\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}. Clearly, we have Ψ⊂Φ⊂(F)red\Psi\subset\Phi\subset(F)_{\red}.

To a congruence is associated a sequence of degrees (a0,…,aν)(a_{0},\dotsc,a_{\nu}) since BB is rationally equivalent to a linear combination of the Schubert cycles of dimension n−1n-1 in the Grassmannian 𝔾⁡(1,n)\mathbb{G}(1,n):

[B]=∑i=0νai​σn−1−i,i[B]=\sum_{i=0}^{\nu}a_{i}\sigma_{n-1-i,i}

(where we set ν:=[n−12]\nu:=\left[\frac{n-1}{2}\right]); in particular, the order a0a_{0} is the number of lines of BB passing through a general point in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, and the class a1a_{1} is the number of lines intersecting a general line LL and contained in a general hyperplane H⊃LH\supset L (i.e. as a Schubert cycle, B⋅σn−2,1B\cdot\sigma_{n-2,1}). a0a_{0} is the degree of f:Λ→ℙnf:\Lambda\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n}: thus if a0>0a_{0}>0, Ψ=Φ\Psi=\Phi, while if a0=1a_{0}=1, set-theoretically, Ψ=Φ=F\Psi=\Phi=F.

An important result—independent of order and class—is the following:

Proposition 1.1 (C. Segre, [Seg88]).

On every line Λb⊂Λ\Lambda_{b}\subset\Lambda of the family, the focal divisor RR either coincides with the whole Λb\Lambda_{b}—in which case Λ⁡(b)\Lambda(b) is called a focal line—or is a zero dimensional subscheme of Λb\Lambda_{b} of length n−1n-1. Moreover, in the latter case, if Λ\Lambda is a first order congruence, Ψ=F\Psi=F and F∩Λ⁡(b)F\cap\Lambda(b) has length n−1n-1.

This result was proven classically in [Seg88]; the first modern proof in the case of the congruences (i.e. families of dimension two) of planes in ℙ4\mathbb{P}^{4} is in [CS92]. See [De 01b], Proposition 1 for a proof of Proposition 1.1.

2. Congruences of lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}

We start with the following result, suggested to us by F. Catanese:

Theorem 2.1.

Let BB be a congruence whose focal locus FF has codimension at least two. Then, BB has order either zero or one.

Proof.

Let us consider the restriction of the map f:Λ→ℙnf:\Lambda\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n} to the set Λ∖f−1​(F)\Lambda\setminus f^{-1}(F). Then, either f−1​(F)=Λf^{-1}(F)=\Lambda, in which case BB is a congruence of order zero, or the map f∣Λ∖f−1​(F)f\mid_{\Lambda\setminus f^{-1}(F)} defines an unramified covering of the set ℙn∖F\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus F. But it is a well-known fact that—by dimensional reasons—ℙn∖F\mathbb{P}^{n}\setminus F is simply connected and Λ∖f−1​(F)\Lambda\setminus f^{-1}(F) is connected. Therefore, f∣Λ∖f−1​(F)f\mid_{\Lambda\setminus f^{-1}(F)} is a homeomorphism, hence ff is a birational map and BB is a first order congruence. ∎

A central definition, introduced in [De 01b], is the notion, ∀d\forall d such that 0≤d≤n−20\leq d\leq n-2, of fundamental dd-locus. This locus ℱd\mathcal{F}^{d}, is so defined: let R1,…,RsR_{1},\dotsc,R_{s} be the horizontal components (i.e. p∣Ri:Ri→Bp_{\mid R_{i}}:R_{i}\rightarrow B is dominant). Now, let Fi:=f⁡(Ri)F_{i}:=f(R_{i}), (as before, we take the schematic image); then, ∀d\forall d such that 0≤d≤n−20\leq d\leq n-2 we define ℱd:=∪dim(Fi)=dFi\mathcal{F}^{d}:=\cup_{\dim(F_{i})=d}F_{i}. By dimensional reasons, the lines of the congruence passing through Pd∈ℱdP_{d}\in\mathcal{F}^{d} form a family of dimension (at least) n−1−dn-1-d (so, set-theoretically, ℱd⊂Φ\mathcal{F}^{d}\subset\Phi).

From this, we infer for example that if the focal locus has dimension zero, then the congruence is a star of lines (see Corollary 1 of [De 01b]). In this article, we will be interested in the subsequent case, i.e. the case in which dim(F)=1\dim(F)=1.

We first note that if our congruence has order one, then there exists a dd such that ℱd≠∅\mathcal{F}^{d}\neq\emptyset.

The first important results of this paper are the following

Theorem 2.2.

Let BB be a congruence of lines in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. If dim(F):=i>0\dim(F):=i>0, then n−12≤i≤n−1\frac{n-1}{2}\leq i\leq n-1. Besides, if i=n−12i=\frac{n-1}{2}, (F)red(F)_{\red} is irreducible and the general line of the congruence meets FF—set-theoretically—in only one point, then FF is—set-theoretically—an ii-plane.

Proof.

Clearly, we have only to prove that dim(F)≥n−12\dim(F)\geq\frac{n-1}{2}. Moreover, by Theorem 2.1, we can reduce to study the cases of order zero and one.

If the congruence has order zero, F=f⁡(Λ)F=f(\Lambda) and FF contains a family of lines of dimension n−1n-1. Then the the observation that among varieties of fixed dimension ii, the projective space is the unique one which contains a family of lines of dimension greater than or equal to 2​(i−1)2(i-1).

Let now suppose that the order is one. Let ℱi\mathcal{F}^{i} be the fundamental ii-locus of maximal dimension i(>0)i(>0). Given i+1i+1 general hyperplanes H0,…,HiH_{0},\dotsc,H_{i} in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} and the corresponding hyperplane sections of ℱi\mathcal{F}^{i}, D0,…,DiD_{0},\dotsc,D_{i}, the lines of Λ\Lambda which meet DjD_{j} form a family of dimension n−2n-2, j=0,…,ij=0,\dotsc,i which will fill a hypersurface MDjM_{D_{j}} in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}. Since D0∩⋯∩Di=∅D_{0}\cap\dotsb\cap D_{i}=\emptyset and M:=MD0∩⋯∩MDi⊂ℙnM:=M_{D_{0}}\cap\dotsb\cap M_{D_{i}}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} is such that dim(M)≥n−1−i≥0\dim(M)\geq n-1-i\geq 0, take Q∈MQ\in M. By definition, there exist ℓi∈Di\ell_{i}\in D_{i} with Q∈ℓiQ\in\ell_{i}. If the ℓi\ell_{i}’s are different, then Q∈FQ\in F. If all ℓi\ell_{i}’s are equal, it is absurd. It follows that M⊂FM\subset F.

Now M⊂FM\subset F; if dim(F)<n−12\dim(F)<\frac{n-1}{2}, then, since dim(M)≥n−1−i\dim(M)\geq n-1-i, we have 2​i>n−12i>n-1, which cannot be, since ℱi⊂F\mathcal{F}^{i}\subset F.

Let us now suppose that the equality holds, D:=(F)redD:=(F)_{\red} is irreducible, and the general line of the congruence meets DD in only one point. If P,Q∈DP,Q\in D are two general points, the set of lines of Λ\Lambda passing through them generate two cones MP,MQ⊂ℙnM_{P},M_{Q}\subset\mathbb{P}^{n} of dimension i+1i+1. Therefore, by our hypotheses dim(MP∩MQ)≥1\dim(M_{P}\cap M_{Q})\geq 1 and MP∩MQM_{P}\cap M_{Q} contains the line joining PP and QQ. So, DD is a linear space. ∎

Proposition 2.3.

Let Λ\Lambda be a congruence in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} and DD the component of the focal locus of maximal dimension i>0i>0; if ℱk\mathcal{F}^{k} is a fundamental kk-locus contained in DD, then n−1−i≤k≤in-1-i\leq k\leq i. In particular, if i=n−12i=\frac{n-1}{2} we have only the ii-fundamental locus ℱi\mathcal{F}^{i}.

Proof.

With notation as in the proof of the preceding theorem, we consider the hyperplane sections of FkF^{k}, D0,…,DkD_{0},\dotsc,D_{k}, for which we have D0∩⋯∩Dk=∅D_{0}\cap\dotsb\cap D_{k}=\emptyset, and so MD0∩⋯∩MDk⊂FM_{D_{0}}\cap\dotsb\cap M_{D_{k}}\subset F. Therefore our thesis easily follows. ∎

Corollary 2.4.

Let Λ\Lambda be a congruence in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}; if dim(F)=1\dim(F)=1, then n≤3n\leq 3.

Remark.

The preceding results are new in the literature, although the method of proof of Theorem 2.2 and Proposition 2.3 is very similar to the respective proofs of Theorem 6 and Corollary 2 of [De 01b]. Actually, in Theorem 6 of [De 01b] we forgot the hypothesis—in the border case i=n−12i=\frac{n-1}{2}—that the general line should meet the focal locus only once.

3. Congruences in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}

Our aim in this article is to classify the congruences with dim(F)=1\dim(F)=1. In view of Corollary 2.4, it is sufficient to consider congruences in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} and ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. The case of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} is well known: all the congruences but the ones of order one (i.e. the pencils) have a focal curve, and the congruence is given by the tangents of the focal curve. Therefore, we will study congruences in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} with dim(F)=1\dim(F)=1. By Theorem 2.1, these are the first order congruences (but the star of lines) of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}, since the order cannot be zero; this can be deduced easily from the fact that the only surface containing a family of dimension two of lines is the plane. Actually, the first order congruences of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} are classified in [Ran86] and [ZILO]. Here we give another easy and—as far as we know—new proof of this classification.

In what follows, we will also call the focal locus fundamental curve.

3.1. Congruences with Irreducible Fundamental Curve

Proposition 3.1.

If the fundamental curve FF of a congruence of lines in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} is irreducible, then we have the following possibilities:

  1. (1)

    if FF is reduced, we are in case (1a) of Theorem 0.1;

  2. (2)

    If FF is non-reduced, we are in case (1b) of Theorem 0.1.

Proof.

First of all, we consider the case of the secant lines of a curve, and we know that we have a first order congruence. We could apply Theorem 2.16 of [De 00] to obtain that deg⁡(F)=3\deg(F)=3, but for the sake of completeness, we will prove this result here. Clearly we have that deg⁡F≥3\deg F\geq 3 for degree reasons. Then, let us denote by aa the class of our congruence, and by rr a general line in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. Let us also denote by VrV_{r} the scroll of the lines of BB meeting rr. An easy application of the Schubert calculus shows that deg⁡(Vr)=a+1\deg(V_{r})=a+1.

Let VrV_{r} and Vr′V_{r^{\prime}} be two such surfaces; we denote by kk the (algebraic) multiplicity of FF in VrV_{r} (and Vr′V_{r^{\prime}}). First of all, we note that the complete intersection of two general surfaces VrV_{r} and Vr′V_{r^{\prime}} is a (reducible) curve Γ\Gamma whose components are the focal locus FF and (a+1)(a+1) lines, i.e. the lines of BB meeting rr and r′r^{\prime}: in fact, a point of Γ\Gamma not belonging to the lines meeting both rr and r′r^{\prime} is a focal point, since through it pass infinitely many lines of BB, i.e. a line meeting rr and another one meeting r′r^{\prime}, and rr and r′r^{\prime} are general. The lines of BB meeting rr and r′r^{\prime} are a+1a+1 since this is the degree of VrV_{r}.

Then, by Bézout, we have that

deg⁡(Vr∩Vr′)\displaystyle\deg(V_{r}\cap V_{r^{\prime}}) =(a+1)2\displaystyle=(a+1)^{2}
=a+1+k2​d\displaystyle=a+1+k^{2}d

—where d:=deg⁡(F)d:=\deg(F)—and we obtain

(1) k2​d=(a+1)​a.k^{2}d=(a+1)a.

Besides, since a line of the congruence not belonging to the (a+1)(a+1) lines meeting rr and r′r^{\prime} must intersect the curve FF in (at least) two points, we deduce

(2) a+1=2​k.a+1=2k.

From formulas (1) and (2) we conclude

k2​(4−d)−2​k=0,k^{2}(4-d)-2k=0,

from which we get the result, i.e. d=3d=3.

So the only possibility is to have the twisted cubic C3C^{3}, which has, in fact, an apparent double point. Since this curve has degree three, the bidegree is (1,3)(1,3).

Then we pass at the other case: by Theorem 2.2, (F)red=:ℓ(F)_{\red}=:\ell is a line; so, if we restrict the congruence to a (general) plane Π\Pi through ℓ\ell, we get a congruence of lines in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} such that its focal locus is contained in ℓ\ell, and therefore it is a pencil of lines with its fundamental point PΠP_{\Pi} in ℓ\ell. Then φ\varphi of Theorem 0.1, (1b) is the map defined by φ⁡(Π)=PΠ\varphi(\Pi)=P_{\Pi}. This congruence has bidegree (1,d)(1,d), as it is easily seen if we consider the lines of the congruence contained in a general plane. ∎

3.2. Congruences with Reducible Fundamental Curve

Proposition 3.2.

If the fundamental curve FF of a first order congruence of lines in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} is reducible, then the congruence is as in Theorem 0.1, case (2).

Proof.

Let us denote by ZZ the 0-dimensional scheme given by F1∩F2F_{1}\cap F_{2} and we set u=length⁡(Z)u=\length(Z).

Let PP be a general point in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}; then, if we set deg⁡(F1):=m1≥m2=:deg⁡(F2)\deg(F_{1}):=m_{1}\geq m_{2}=:\deg(F_{2}), the cone given by the join P​FjPF_{j} has degree mjm_{j}; as usual, by Bézout

deg⁡(P​F1∩P​F2)=m1​m2.\deg(PF_{1}\cap PF_{2})=m_{1}m_{2}.

Since we have a congruence of order one, we obtain:

(3) u=m1​m2−1;u=m_{1}m_{2}-1;

this is due to the fact that only one of the lines of P​F1∩P​F2PF_{1}\cap PF_{2} is a line of the congruence; therefore the others must be the uu lines of the join P​ZPZ.

If QQ is a general point of F1F_{1}, there will pass m2​(m1−1)m_{2}(m_{1}-1) secant lines of F1F_{1} through QQ meeting F2F_{2} also; but these lines will pass through the points of ZZ, since if one of these lines did not intersect ZZ, this line would be a focal line, and varying these lines when we vary QQ on F1F_{1}, we would obtain a focal surface. Besides, since QQ is general, we can suppose that it does not belong to the tangent cones of the two curves at the points of ZZ. Then we have that

(4) u=(m1−1)​m2,u=(m_{1}-1)m_{2},

and by equation (3) we obtain m2=1m_{2}=1, u=m1−1u=m_{1}-1. To see that F1F_{1} is a rational curve, we can simply project it from a general point of the line F2F_{2} onto a plane: by the Clebsh formula, the projected curve has geometric genus zero.

The class is—as usual—calculated intersecting with a general plane. ∎

3.3. Final Remarks about First Order Congruences

We finish this article analysing which of these congruences are smooth as surfaces in the Grassmannian 𝔾⁡(1,3)\mathbb{G}(1,3).

Proposition 3.3.

The smooth first order congruences of lines BB in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} are

  1. (1)

    the secants of the twisted cubic, in which case BB is the Veronese surface;

  2. (2)

    the join of a line and a smooth conic meeting in a point, in which case BB is a rational normal cubic scroll;

  3. (3)

    the join of two—non-meeting—lines in which case BB is a quadric.

Proof.

We see from [AG93] and [ABT94] that the only possible bidegrees for a smooth congruence in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} with a fundamental curve are (1,1)(1,1), (1,2)(1,2), (1,3)(1,3) and (3,6)(3,6). The last case can be excluded because has order three, by Theorem 0.1. From the description of these congruence given in [AS92] we get the proposition. ∎

Remark.

Observe that, if the fundamental curve is non-reduced, its support is a line ℓ\ell. Its image in 𝔾⁡(1,3)\mathbb{G}(1,3) is a singular point LL for BB: more precisely, BB is a 22-dimensional linear section, tangent to 𝔾⁡(1,3)\mathbb{G}(1,3) at LL.

We observe finally that the case of two lines is the one in which BB is the intersection of the two tangent hyperplane sections of the Grassmannian corresponding to the two lines, i.e. BB is a general 22-dimensional linear section of 𝔾⁡(1,3)\mathbb{G}(1,3). From this description we see that the case in which the fundamental curve is a line only is a limit case of this one, when the two lines coincide.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
